newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: S.Africa union employment demands seen premature.
newsitem.headline: S.Africa union employment demands seen premature.

text.p: South African labour officials said on Monday they were committed to new legislation that delayed union demands for the working week to be reduced to 40 hours and maternity leave set at six months.
Labour department minimum standards director Lisa Seftel said that the government was committed to seeing both aims introduced in the long term but "it is not appropriate to legislate that now."

Instead, the Employment Standards Bill would stipulate a 45 hour working week and four months maternity leave despite objections by the Congress of South African Trade Unions (Cosatu), which plans a national strike on June 2 to protest against the bill.

The bill was tabled by cabinet in April and still has to pass through parliament but an impasse has been reached between labour, business and government in the National Economic Development and Labour Council (Nedlac) on some fundamental issues.
Seftel said however negotiations on the bill were continuing. Asked if differences could be resolved before June 2, she said that "anything is possible in negotiations."
Labour department legal adviser Paul Benjamin said that the working week for South African workers ranged from about 39 to 40 hours in the most organised industries.
In agriculture and mining the norm was 48 hours while security workers worked up to 60 hours a week.
"In the well organised manufacturing sector, where there is the most detailed information, the norm is between 41 and 43 and in the metal industry it is 45," Benjamin said.
"So the purpose of this bill is to bring those who are lagging behind up to the norms that have been achieved in more organised sectors," he added.

In agriculture and mining, the reduction of the working week from 48 to 45 hours would take place six months after the bill went into effect and for security guards the reduction from 60 hours to 45 would be phased in 30 months after the bill was enacted.
Seftel and Benjamin said it had been decided to set paid maternity leave at four rather than six months because six months could be a disincentive to employ women of child bearing age.

A task team had been established to determine how workers should be paid during maternity leave, possibly through the Unemployment Insurance Fund, because some sectors would face a greater burden than others.
